props.title: E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial
props.initialSlug: A friendship that's out of this world.

sections.content: E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial (1982) revolutionized family sci-fi by grounding otherworldly wonder in authentic childhood emotion. Spielberg masterfully captures suburban life through a kid's-eye view, much like his earlier Close Encounters of the Third Kind (1977). The film's genius lies in making E.T. not just an alien, but a best friend - scared, curious, and loving. The bike flight scene, scored perfectly by John Williams, became instantly iconic and influenced countless films like The NeverEnding Story (1984) and Super 8 (2011) that aimed to capture that same magical realism.

sections.content: The film's impact on 80s kid-centered sci-fi can't be overstated. The Last Mimzy (2007) and Earth to Echo (2014) directly borrowed its "kids protect alien friend from government" plot. But E.T.'s lasting power comes from Spielberg's refusal to talk down to children. The film tackles divorce, loneliness, and loss through Elliott's perspective. The government agents aren't cartoonish villains - they're threatening because they represent adult authority that doesn't understand childhood imagination and loyalty.

Cinematographer Allen Daviau's low camera angles revolutionized how films visually represent children's perspectives. This technique influenced later classics like The Goonies (1985) and Stand By Me (1986). The practical effects by Carlo Rambaldi hold up remarkably well, proving that emotional authenticity matters more than technical perfection. E.T.'s expressive face and movements created a template for how to make audiences empathize with non-human characters, seen later in films like WALL-E (2008). SUBHEAD: Impact on Modern Family Sci-Fi

movies.title: Batteries Not Included
movies.slug: Small alien machines help residents save their apartment building from demolition

sections.content: While modern family sci-fi relies heavily on CGI, films like The Iron Giant (1999) and How to Train Your Dragon (2010) follow E.T.'s emotional blueprint - the friendship between a lonely child and a misunderstood non-human character. Big Hero 6 (2014) particularly echoes E.T.'s themes of loss and healing through an otherworldly friendship. Even darker sci-fi like Midnight Special (2016) draws from E.T.'s government pursuit storyline while exploring parent-child bonds.
